rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown compounds across the full solvent-strength range while keeping analysis efficient. This should reveal how many compounds elute early versus late and whether subsequent runs should be weaker/stronger, shorter/longer, or cooler/hotter.

All 10 compounds are already fully observed with excellent resolution, so the limiting factor is analysis time rather than separation. A shorter gradient should pull the well-resolved cluster earlier and improve CRF while likely retaining acceptable minimum resolution.

The 12 min gradient is fast but compresses the central cluster too much, with one sub-1.5 pair limiting the resolution term. A small increase to 14 min should selectively decompress that region while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a high overall CRF.

Resolution of the critical pair improves as tG increases, and at 14 min it is close to the likely threshold while still incurring no time penalty. Testing 16 min should push that pair into safer separation and may further raise the resolution term while likely staying within the zero time-penalty window.

Since tG 15 is unavailable, adjust temperature instead to fine-tune the critical pair while preserving the near-optimal 14 min timing. A slightly lower temperature may increase selectivity in the crowded middle cluster enough to improve the resolution term without introducing a time penalty.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity in the central cluster, so the complementary test is a modest increase above 40 C at the near-optimal 14 min gradient. This may improve the critical spacing enough to outperform the current best while keeping the run in the no-time-penalty region.

Temperature changes away from 40 C hurt selectivity, so stay at 40 C and probe a slightly longer gradient than 16 min. This will test whether the resolution gain around the critical pair can outweigh the modest added time and surpass the current best.

The optimum is clearly near 14–16 min at 40 C, but all tests so far used the steepest endpoint. Lowering phi1 slightly may flatten the gradient in the crowded midrange, improving the critical pair around peaks 6–7 without much effect on total run time because the last peak is already well before the end.

Dropping phi1 to 0.90 improved the critical pair at 14 min and gave the best CRF so far, suggesting a flatter effective gradient helps. A 16 min version should test whether a bit more decompression can raise the resolution term to 1.000 while keeping the time penalty small enough to beat 0.989.

With phi1 = 0.90, the critical pair improved versus 0.95 but still limits the resolution term slightly while the run remains comfortably short. Lowering phi1 one more step at the same 14 min and 40 C should further flatten the gradient in the crowded region and may lift the critical pair above the threshold without incurring a time penalty.

The best region is clearly around phi1 0.90 and 14 min, but the remaining opportunity is to see whether a slightly shorter run can preserve enough of the improved selectivity to beat the current best on time. Testing 12 min at phi1 0.90 directly checks that local tradeoff around the current optimum.

The remaining lever near the optimum is the starting strength: raising phi0 slightly will flatten the gradient slope over the key midrange while sacrificing little because the earliest peaks are still well retained and highly resolved. This may selectively open the persistent 6/7 critical pair enough to reach the maximum CRF.

Injection 12 is very close to ideal, and the persistent limitation is still the 6/7 pair. Lowering phi1 one step while keeping the improved phi0 may further flatten the effective gradient around that cluster and could push the resolution term to 1.000 while staying near the same short run time.

The maximum score is already achieved, so this run is only to probe robustness near the optimum. Increasing phi0 one step tests whether a slightly shallower gradient with even weaker early retention still preserves the perfect CRF plateau.

A second distinct method has also achieved the maximum CRF, and increasing phi0 reduced run time while preserving full resolution. Testing one more step higher maps the extent of this optimum plateau and may identify an even faster fully optimal method.

The optimum plateau includes phi0 0.15, phi1 0.85, and pushing phi0 higher began to erode the critical pair. Lowering phi1 one step from that successful point may retain the good balance while slightly flattening the mid-gradient further, testing whether the perfect-score plateau extends in that direction too.

You already have multiple methods at the maximum CRF, so the best remaining use of injections is mapping the plateau around those optima. Testing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 checks whether lowering both endpoints together keeps perfect resolution with no time penalty.

The 1.000 plateau appears centered near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, with lower phi1 adding time cost and higher phi0 risking loss of critical-pair resolution. Testing phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.90 probes the remaining adjacent corner of that local optimum region.

You already have multiple 1.000 methods at 14 min, so a sensible remaining question is whether the same successful composition window can support a shorter gradient without losing too much critical-pair resolution. Testing the known-optimal solvent range at 12 min directly probes whether a faster perfect method exists.

Since phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.85 was also fully optimal at 14 min, shortening that slightly stronger-starting version is the most informative remaining speed test. If it preserves the critical pair better than the 0.10/0.85/12 method, it could reveal a broader fast-optimum region even though the maximum score is already reached.

The objective is already maximized, so remaining injections can only explore robustness around the optimum. A cooler version of one 1.000 method checks how sensitive the perfect plateau is to temperature at otherwise optimal gradient settings.

Cooling an otherwise optimal method strongly degraded selectivity, so the complementary robustness check is a modest increase above 40 C at the same optimal composition and gradient time. This will define temperature sensitivity on the high side while staying close to the proven optimum.

The optimum is clearly centered at 40 C, but with only a few injections left the most useful remaining information is whether the second 1.000 composition shows the same low-temperature fragility. This checks robustness of the other optimal point without changing the already validated gradient shape.

The 35 C test showed the second optimal composition also loses selectivity when cooled, so the symmetric high-temperature check is the last useful robustness probe. This completes the temperature bracket around a known 1.000 method while staying at the already validated gradient settings.

The maximum CRF has already been achieved, so the final injection is best used to map one last nearby condition not yet tested. This combination probes whether the stronger flattening from phi1 0.80 can be balanced by a longer gradient to maintain full resolution, completing the local design space around the optimum plateau.
